paragraphs.heading: The color of the powder
paragraphs.text: A mineral's streak is the color of the powder it leaves when it is dragged across an unweathered surface. That surface is called a streak plate, and it is generally made of unglazed porcelain tile. Without a streak plate, the unglazed bottom of a porcelain bowl or vase will work, and so will the back of a glazed tile. If the mineral seems to make no streak, its streak is said to be white or colorless.

paragraphs.heading: Why geologists trust it
paragraphs.text: For most minerals, the apparent color can vary considerably. The finely ground powder in a streak generally keeps a more consistent color that is characteristic of the mineral. This makes streak an important diagnostic tool for identifying minerals. It is particularly important for opaque and colored materials.

paragraphs.heading: Why powder is steadier
paragraphs.text: Trace impurities, or a disturbed large-scale crystal structure, can make a mineral's apparent color vary widely. A small amount of an impurity that strongly absorbs one particular wavelength can radically change which wavelengths of light the specimen reflects, and so change its apparent color. Dragging the specimen to make a streak breaks it into microscopic crystals that point in random directions. In that state, small impurities do not greatly affect how light is absorbed.

paragraphs.heading: The hardness limit
paragraphs.text: The trail comes from the mineral being crushed into powder, so a streak can only be made with minerals softer than the streak plate, which is around 7 on the Mohs scale of mineral hardness. For harder minerals, a small sample can be filed or crushed to find the powder's color, and the result is then usually rubbed on a streak plate. Most of these harder minerals have an unhelpful white streak. Streak is also less useful for silicate minerals, as most of them either leave a white streak or are too hard to be powdered easily.

paragraphs.heading: Matches and surprises
paragraphs.text: With some minerals the streak is similar to the natural color; cinnabar, lazurite and native gold are examples. Others leave surprising colors. Fluorite can appear as purple, blue, yellow or green crystals, yet its streak is always white. Hematite looks black but leaves a red streak, which accounts for its name, taken from the Greek word "haima", meaning blood. Galena can look similar to hematite, but its gray streak makes it easy to tell apart.
